did_you_know.text: The phrase “in the days to come” does not necessarily mean only the end of the world; it can also describe the future and what will happen to later generations.
In the ancient world, the firstborn usually had special rights in inheritance and leadership. That is why Reuben’s loss of status is especially significant.

Later in the Bible, Simeon is described as receiving territory within Judah’s inheritance, while Levi receives cities scattered among the tribes of Israel. This may be seen as an echo of the promise, “I will divide them in Jacob.”
The name Judah is connected in the Bible with the root y-d-h, associated with giving thanks. The name therefore also carries the idea of gratitude.

The word shevet can mean both a ruler’s staff and a tribal group, while meḥoqeq refers to a leader or lawgiver. The word “Shiloh” in this verse has received different interpretations throughout history.
The image of tying a donkey to a vine and washing clothes in wine is poetic imagery for great agricultural abundance, not practical advice.

When the tribes’ territories are described later, Zebulun is located in Lower Galilee, not directly on the Mediterranean coast. Some interpreters therefore understand the verse as referring also to trade connections and access to sea routes.
In the middle of the blessings, a brief and direct prayer to God suddenly appears. It creates a moment of hope and a request for rescue amid the descriptions of the future.
Joseph is compared to a fruitful plant whose branches grow over a wall. The word “daughters” here may refer poetically to branches or shoots of the plant.
The Cave of Machpelah is presented as a place legally purchased from Ephron the Hittite, not merely chosen without an established claim. This emphasizes the family’s foothold in the land of Canaan.
The verse uses two expressions connected with death: “he breathed his last” and “he was gathered to his people.” “Gathered to his people” is a biblical expression for joining earlier generations.
